title: Syntriod: A Robust Initial Parameter Estimator for Radial Velocity Curve Solutions Beyond Conventional Sampling Limits
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures and 3 tables. Published in Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific (PASP). Code will be made available on GitHub soon
summary:
We present Syntriod, an orbital-phase domain radial velocity (RV) template-based algorithm designed to provide robust initial orbital parameter estimates for spectroscopic binaries across diverse observational sampling conditions. Rather than performing full orbital inference, Syntriod constrains the parameter space with physically consistent solutions to guide subsequent optimization procedures.
  We evaluate its performance using 10,000 synthetic Keplerian orbits spanning diverse configurations and sampling regimes. For well-sampled datasets ($N_{obs} \ge 8$), Syntriod recovers orbital periods with relative accuracies of order $10^{-3}$. At the theoretical sampling limit ($N_{obs} = 6$), the method maintains a ~94% success rate, while classical period-search techniques like Lomb-Scargle become increasingly affected by aliasing. Even below this limit ($N_{obs} = 5$), Syntriod recovers the correct orbital solution in ~83% of cases, showing gradual degradation rather than catastrophic failure.
  We further evaluate the method on 12 real spectroscopic binary systems (HD 160934, Phi Cyg, Capella A, Kepler 16, KIC 3858884, KIC 6867766, KIC 2445134, KIC 3003991, DU Boo, HL Dra, FP Boo, and AK Her) spanning broad orbital periods and eccentricities. Syntriod consistently reproduces literature solutions even when datasets are randomly subsampled to sparse regimes. Where a full Keplerian solution becomes underconstrained ($N_{obs} \le 4$), the algorithm transitions to linear dynamical relations, recovering parameters such as mass ratio ($q$) and systemic velocity ($γ$) with success rates exceeding 99%.
  These results demonstrate that Syntriod provides reliable, computationally efficient initial parameter estimates across well-sampled and sparse regimes, making it a practical pre-solver for modern orbit-fitting pipelines and large spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: Syntriod is an orbital-phase domain RV template algorithm that provides robust initial orbital parameter estimates for spectroscopic binaries, performing well even at the theoretical sampling limit and transitioning to linear dynamical relations when Keplerian solutions are underconstrained.
AI.motivation: To provide robust initial orbital parameter estimates for spectroscopic binaries that can guide subsequent optimization, avoiding the need for full orbital inference and handling diverse, sparse observational sampling where classical methods like Lomb-Scargle suffer from aliasing.
AI.method: Syntriod uses an orbital-phase domain radial velocity template-based approach that constrains the parameter space with physically consistent solutions. It evaluates performance on 10,000 synthetic Keplerian orbits and 12 real spectroscopic binary systems, testing across various observational sampling densities from well-sampled (N_obs ≥ 8) to sparse (N_obs ≤ 4) regimes.
AI.result: For well-sampled datasets (N_obs ≥ 8), Syntriod recovers orbital periods with ~10^{-3} relative accuracy. At the theoretical sampling limit (N_obs=6), it maintains ~94% success rate vs Lomb-Scargle's aliasing issues. Even at N_obs=5, ~83% success rate. On 12 real binaries, it reproduces literature solutions under random subsampling. For N_obs ≤ 4, it transitions to linear dynamical relations recovering q and γ with >99% success.
AI.conclusion: Syntriod provides reliable, computationally efficient initial parameter estimates across both well-sampled and sparse regimes, making it a practical pre-solver for modern orbit-fitting pipelines and large spectroscopic surveys.

title: Investigating the Observational Progenitor Mass Gap in the White Dwarf Initial-Final Mass Relation. I. Cluster Census and Characterization of the First White Dwarfs in the Gap
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: In recent years, Gaia has been the primary driver of the expansion of the white dwarf (WD) initial-final mass relation (IFMR) in open clusters. The increased sample size has highlighted a pronounced observational gap at progenitor masses of $\simeq2$--$2.7\,M_\odot$, with no spectroscopically confirmed cluster-member WDs in this range. Analysis of the Milky Way open cluster census shows that this absence is primarily driven by the scarcity of appropriately aged, nearby clusters capable of hosting Gaia-detectable WDs, implying that deeper, targeted photometry will be required to build a substantial sample in this progenitor mass range. We further searched for previously unexamined Gaia WD candidates in clusters with ages consistent with producing gap progenitors and identified two viable targets, which we observed spectroscopically with Gemini GMOS-N. Both targets yield inferred progenitor masses within the observational gap, making them the first spectroscopically confirmed cluster-member WDs in this progenitor mass range. The NGC 6991 candidate, in particular, is confirmed as a DA WD with an inferred progenitor mass of $2.12^{+0.04}_{-0.15}\,M_\odot$, providing further support for a non-monotonic trend in the IFMR.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia data and Gemini spectroscopy, this study identifies the first spectroscopically confirmed white dwarfs in open clusters within the previously empty progenitor mass gap of ~2–2.7 M☉, with one object (NGC 6991) supporting a non-monotonic initial-final mass relation.
AI.motivation: To address the pronounced observational gap in the white dwarf initial-final mass relation at progenitor masses of ~2–2.7 M☉, where no spectroscopically confirmed cluster-member WDs existed despite Gaia's extensive survey of open clusters.
AI.method: Analyzed the Milky Way open cluster census to explain the observational gap; searched for previously unexamined Gaia WD candidates in appropriately aged clusters; performed spectroscopic follow-up with Gemini GMOS-N on two viable targets.
AI.result: Confirmed the first two spectroscopically identified cluster-member WDs within the gap progenitor mass range. The NGC 6991 candidate is a DA WD with inferred progenitor mass 2.12+0.04−0.15 M☉.
AI.conclusion: The gap is primarily due to scarcity of suitably aged nearby clusters; deeper targeted photometry is needed for larger samples. The NGC 6991 result supports a non-monotonic IFMR trend, challenging simpler monotonic models.

title: A Test of FeH Line Parameters using DR19 APOGEE spectra of Benchmark M Dwarfs
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures and 5 tables
summary: Recent studies have suggested a mismatch of up to 0.20 dex between iron abundances derived from Fe I and FeH lines in the H-band spectra of M dwarfs, and in this work we investigate the nature of this possible offset. We analyze near-infrared H-band APOGEE spectra of stars in 18 binaries composed of a G-dwarf primary and an M-dwarf secondary, together with four M-dwarf stars having measured angular diameters from the literature, and six M-dwarf members of the Hyades and Coma Berenices open clusters. These three families of benchmarks were used to evaluate the FeH line list and check for possible systematic uncertainties in the FeH $gf$-values. Our tests used 1-D LTE plane-parallel model atmospheres, a radiative transfer code, and the baseline APOGEE spectral line list to derive metallicities for the binary G-dwarf primaries using Fe I lines, while stellar parameters and metallicities for the M dwarfs used both FeH and Fe I lines. The mean metallicity obtained for the Hyades M-dwarfs was $\langle$[Fe/H]$\rangle$=+0.08$\pm$0.04, and for Coma Berenices $\langle$[Fe/H]$\rangle$=+0.02$\pm$0.08. The metallicities of the G- and M-dwarfs in binary systems showed excellent agreement (0.06 dex), and the mean metallicities for the open clusters were also consistent with literature values from high-resolution optical analyses. We investigated the consistency between the spectroscopic and interferometric $T_{\rm eff}$ scales, finding agreement within the uncertainties. Forcing full agreement between the spectroscopic and interferometric $T_{\rm eff}$ scales resulted in a poorer match for the metallicities in the binaries and the open clusters. We conclude that the best overall concordance is obtained when no adjustments are made to the FeH $gf$-values, which are based on the Hargreaves et al. (2010) line list.

AI.tldr: This study investigates a reported ~0.20 dex discrepancy between Fe I and FeH iron abundances in M dwarfs using APOGEE H-band spectra of G+M binaries, M dwarfs with measured angular diameters, and open cluster members. By testing FeH line lists with 1-D LTE plane-parallel models, the authors find no systematic offset—metallicities from G and M dwarfs in binaries agree to 0.06 dex, and open cluster results match literature values. The best overall consistency is achieved without adjusting the FeH gf-values from the Hargreaves et al. (2010) line list.
AI.motivation: Previous studies reported a possible mismatch of up to 0.20 dex between iron abundances derived from Fe I and FeH lines in M dwarfs, and this work aims to investigate whether this offset is real or due to systematic uncertainties in the FeH line list.
AI.method: The authors analyzed APOGEE H-band spectra of 18 G-dwarf+M-dwarf binaries, four M dwarfs with measured angular diameters, and six M dwarfs in Hyades and Coma Berenices open clusters. They used 1-D LTE plane-parallel model atmospheres with a radiative transfer code and the baseline APOGEE spectral line list, deriving metallicities for G dwarfs from Fe I lines and for M dwarfs from both FeH and Fe I lines.
AI.result: Metallicities from G and M dwarfs in binaries show excellent agreement (0.06 dex). Hyades M-dwarfs yield ⟨[Fe/H]⟩=+0.08±0.04, Coma Berenices ⟨[Fe/H]⟩=+0.02±0.08, consistent with literature. Spectroscopic and interferometric Teff scales agree within uncertainties; forcing full agreement worsens binary and cluster metallicity matches.
AI.conclusion: The best overall concordance is obtained when no adjustments are made to the FeH gf-values based on the Hargreaves et al. (2010) line list, indicating no significant systematic offset between Fe I and FeH iron abundances in M dwarfs.

title: Empirical H- and K-band Limb Darkening for 31 CHARA Stars: A Near-Infrared Benchmark for Stellar-Atmosphere Models
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal; 16 figures, 6 tables and 28 pages
summary: Limb darkening, the decrease in stellar intensity from the disk center to the limb, encodes the temperature structure and opacity of stellar atmospheres. Direct spatially resolved measurements of this center-to-limb variation remain scarce, especially in the near-infrared. We present interferometric limb-darkening measurements for 31 stars observed simultaneously in the $H$ and $K$ bands with the CHARA Array. The sample spans spectral types F--M and luminosity classes IV--I. The targets are well resolved in $H$ and, for most targets, also in $K$. This coverage constrains the visibility curvature associated with limb darkening in joint $H+K$ fits. We fit the combined $H{+}K$ squared visibilities with four analytic limb-darkening laws and compare the resulting coefficients with bandpass-matched predictions from five stellar-atmosphere grids (Kurucz, MPS1, MPS2, Stagger, and spherical SATLAS, with reported coefficients placed on the Rosseland-radius convention) spanning one-dimensional plane-parallel, three-dimensional radiation--hydrodynamic, and spherical low-gravity models. The associated limb-darkened angular diameters are measured with median formal precisions of $\simeq 0.2$--0.3\%. The CHARA results show expected weaker limb darkening at longer wavelengths and also with increasing $T_{\rm eff}$. The clearest discrepancy with the atmosphere grids is in the wavelength dependence: the median fractional decrease in the power-law coefficient from $H$ to $K$ is $\simeq 39\%$ in the CHARA sample, compared with only $\simeq 17$--$22\%$ with model predictions. Relative to the MPS2 comparison, the empirical coefficients are higher by $\simeq 21\%$ in $H$ and lower by $\simeq 5\%$ in $K$. These results provide multi-band interferometric limb darkening as a near-infrared benchmark for stellar-atmosphere models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents interferometric limb-darkening measurements for 31 stars (F–M spectral types, IV–I luminosity classes) using CHARA Array H and K bands, fitting four analytic limb-darkening laws and comparing with five stellar-atmosphere model grids. Key findings include systematic discrepancies in wavelength dependence: the power-law coefficient decreases ~39% from H to K band empirically versus only ~17–22% in models. Empirical coefficients are ~21% higher in H and ~5% lower in K than MPS2 predictions.
AI.motivation: Direct spatially resolved limb-darkening measurements, especially in the near-infrared, remain scarce. Such empirical benchmarks are critical for validating stellar-atmosphere models, which underpin precise stellar parameter determination, exoplanet characterization, and interferometric imaging.
AI.method: 31 stars were observed simultaneously in H and K bands with the CHARA Array interferometer. Combined H+K squared visibilities were fitted with four analytic limb-darkening laws. The derived coefficients were compared with bandpass-matched predictions from five stellar-atmosphere grids (Kurucz, MPS1, MPS2, Stagger, spherical SATLAS) spanning 1D plane-parallel, 3D radiation-hydrodynamic, and spherical low-gravity models, with coefficients placed on the Rosseland-radius convention.
AI.result: Limb-darkened angular diameters measured with ~0.2–0.3% formal precision. Empirical limb darkening is weaker at longer wavelengths and with increasing Teff. The median fractional decrease in the power-law coefficient from H to K is ~39% empirically versus ~17–22% in model predictions. Compared to MPS2, empirical coefficients are ~21% higher in H and ~5% lower in K.
AI.conclusion: These multi-band interferometric results serve as a near-infrared benchmark for stellar-atmosphere models, revealing systematic discrepancies in the wavelength dependence of limb darkening that models currently fail to reproduce.

title: Localized magnetic pressure anisotropy in strange dwarfs with crystalline crusts
summary: We study equilibrium sequences of magnetized strange dwarfs composed of a self bound MIT bag strange matter core, with \(B_{\rm bag}^{1/4}=145\,{\rm MeV}\), and an ordinary crystalline crust. The aim is to determine how nuclear composition changes and magnetic pressure anisotropy in the crust modify the mass radius relation. The strange core is kept isotropic, while the crust is described either by pure nuclei stopped at the first inverse beta threshold or by electron capture sequences extended to neutron drip for C, O, Ne, and Mg compositions; selected mixed crusts are also considered up to the first instability. The stellar structure is solved with the radial pressure as the integrated pressure and with the anisotropic contribution \(2(P_t-P_r)/r\) restricted to the crust. This treatment is compared with ordinary white dwarf sequences and with scalar pressure branch calculations. We find that extending the crust to neutron drip produces more compact strange dwarf branches than stopping at the inverse beta threshold, because the evolved crust is softer and the core crust transition occurs at higher pressure. Magnetic anisotropy further shifts the selected branches toward smaller radii, with the effect visible across the compositions studied and clearer at fixed stellar mass. The comparison with compact objects from the Montreal White Dwarf Database is used only as an observational reference plane, but it indicates that compact white dwarf candidates are a relevant region for testing small core strange dwarf scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper studies magnetized strange dwarfs with a strange matter core and crystalline crust, finding that extending the crust to neutron drip and adding magnetic anisotropy produces more compact configurations, relevant for testing compact white dwarf candidates.
AI.motivation: To determine how nuclear composition changes and magnetic pressure anisotropy in the crust modify the mass-radius relation of strange dwarfs, and to identify observational signatures for testing such compact object scenarios.
AI.method: Equilibrium sequences of strange dwarfs are computed with an MIT bag strange matter core (B_bag^{1/4}=145 MeV) and a crystalline crust. Crust compositions include pure nuclei at inverse beta threshold, extended electron capture sequences to neutron drip for C, O, Ne, Mg, and selected mixed crusts. Stellar structure is solved with radial pressure and anisotropic term 2(P_t-P_r)/r restricted to the crust, compared with ordinary WD sequences and scalar pressure branches.
AI.result: Extending crust to neutron drip yields more compact strange dwarf branches than stopping at inverse beta threshold due to softer crust and higher core-crust transition pressure. Magnetic anisotropy further shifts branches toward smaller radii across all compositions. Comparison with Montreal White Dwarf Database shows compact WD candidates are relevant for testing small core strange dwarf scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Both extended crust compositions and magnetic anisotropy significantly reduce strange dwarf radii, making compact white dwarf candidates promising targets for observational tests of strange dwarf models with small strange cores.

title: Magnetic pressure anisotropy in ultra-dense white dwarfs: Landau quantization and neutronization effects
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures and 2 tables
summary: Strong magnetic fields modify the thermodynamics of white dwarf (WD) matter by quantizing the transverse motion of degenerate electrons into Landau levels and splitting the pressure into components parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field. We investigate how this microscopic pressure anisotropy affects ultra-dense WD sequences when Coulomb lattice contributions, electron capture thresholds, neutron drip limits, and nuclear composition are treated consistently in the equation of state (EoS). The stellar equilibrium structure is obtained by solving an anisotropic extension of the Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) equations, where $P_r = P_\parallel$ and $P_t = P_\perp$ denote the radial and tangential pressures, respectively. We compare the post-electron-capture branches with their corresponding pre-capture sequences for pure $^{12}\rm{C}$, $^{16}\rm{O}$, $^{20}\rm{Ne}$, and $^{24}\rm{Mg}$ compositions, as well as for fixed 50/50 C/O, Ne/O, and Mg/Ne mixtures. The EoS predicts $P_\perp < P_\parallel$ in density ranges where only a few Landau levels are occupied. Consequently, pressure anisotropy shifts the stellar sequences toward smaller radii, with only minor changes in the maximum masses. We also find that post-capture configurations cannot be interpreted from the mass--radius plane alone, since the corresponding $M(ρ_c)$ curves reveal unstable portions after the maximum mass is reached. Our results show that strong magnetic fields significantly reduce the radii of low-mass WDs, yielding better agreement with the observational data available in the Montreal White Dwarf Database and suggesting that future high-precision observations of massive magnetic WDs could help assess the role of magnetic pressure anisotropy in determining their masses and radii.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how strong magnetic fields create pressure anisotropy (parallel vs. perpendicular components) in white dwarf matter, and how this affects stellar structure by solving anisotropic TOV equations. The authors find that anisotropy shifts sequences toward smaller radii (better matching observations) while only slightly affecting maximum masses, and that post-electron-capture configurations can't be interpreted solely from mass-radius diagrams.
AI.motivation: To understand how microscopic magnetic pressure anisotropy—due to Landau quantization of electron motion in strong magnetic fields—affects the global structure and stability of ultra-dense white dwarfs, especially when coupled with realistic physics including Coulomb lattice effects, electron capture, neutron drip, and nuclear composition.
AI.method: The authors solve anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations with radial pressure P_r = P_∥ and tangential pressure P_t = P_⊥, using an equation of state that consistently includes Landau quantization, Coulomb lattice contributions, electron capture thresholds, and neutron drip limits for various pure compositions (¹²C, ¹⁶O, ²⁰Ne, ²⁴Mg) and fixed mixtures (50/50 C/O, Ne/O, Mg/Ne).
AI.result: The EoS shows P_⊥ < P_∥ when few Landau levels are occupied. Pressure anisotropy shifts WD sequences to smaller radii with only minor changes to maximum masses. Post-capture configurations cannot be interpreted from the mass-radius plane alone as their M(ρ_c) curves show unstable portions after the maximum mass. Strong magnetic fields significantly reduce low-mass WD radii, matching Montreal White Dwarf Database observations better.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic pressure anisotropy is a crucial ingredient for modeling magnetized white dwarfs, as it produces smaller radii consistent with observations. Future high-precision observations of massive magnetic WDs could help test the role of magnetic pressure anisotropy in determining masses and radii.

title: A Systematic Study of Quiescent and Outburst Properties of X-ray-bright Young Stellar Objects Using XMM-Newton
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) exhibit strong X-ray emission, widely attributed to magnetic reconnection and magnetospheric accretion; however, owing primarily to limited photon statistics, observational tests of these mechanisms have often relied on simplified analyses, leaving room for more precise constraints on their emission processes. We aim to derive the X-ray properties of X-ray-bright YSOs selected from multiple star clusters and investigate their emission mechanisms through an approach from multiple perspectives based on timing and spectroscopic analysis. We performed a systematic search of XMM-Newton archival observations and constructed a sample of 51 X-ray-bright YSOs for timing and spectroscopic analyses. We identified quiescent and outburst phases through timing analysis, performed phase-resolved multi-temperature spectroscopy. Multi-temperature plasma structures are detected in both quiescent and outburst emission. The relationships among the timing and spectral parameters are broadly consistent with a magnetic-reconnection scenario. Comparison with Gaia DR3 stellar parameters suggests that magnetospheric accretion alone has difficulty explaining most of the fitted X-ray temperatures, although the coolest model components with $kT \lesssim 0.3$ keV may include an accretion-shock contribution. After separating these low-temperature components, the remaining quiescent components show a clearer positive correlation in the $EM$--$kT$ plane, with magnetic-loop lengths distributed around $10^{12}$ cm. Neupert-like behavior, the temporal evolution of temperature and emission measure, the Rossby-number activity relation, and positive correlations between quiescent and outburst properties all suggest that magnetic reconnection plays a key role in both phases.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes X-ray properties of 51 X-ray-bright YSOs from XMM-Newton archival data, finding that magnetic reconnection dominates emission in both quiescent and outburst phases, with magnetospheric accretion contributing only to the coolest plasma components (kT ≲ 0.3 keV).
AI.motivation: YSOs exhibit strong X-ray emission attributed to magnetic reconnection and magnetospheric accretion, but limited photon statistics have prevented precise observational constraints on these emission mechanisms.
AI.method: Systematic search of XMM-Newton archival data to construct a sample of 51 X-ray-bright YSOs; performed timing analysis to identify quiescent/outburst phases, phase-resolved multi-temperature spectroscopy, and comparison with Gaia DR3 parameters.
AI.result: Multi-temperature plasma structures detected in both phases; relationships among parameters consistent with magnetic reconnection; coolest components (kT ≲ 0.3 keV) may include accretion-shock contribution; magnetic-loop lengths ~10^12 cm; Neupert-like behavior and positive correlations support magnetic reconnection in both phases.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic reconnection plays a key role in both quiescent and outburst X-ray emission from YSOs, while magnetospheric accretion contributes only to the lowest-temperature components.

title: Decay Length of Slow Magnetoacoustic Waves in the Solar Corona using SDO/AIA and SolO/EUI
comment: Accepted for publication in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A
summary: Slow magnetoacoustic waves have been observed in the solar corona for decades; yet, existing theories do not fully explain the wide range of observed decay lengths, and measurements from different instruments frequently disagree. We present two events with simultaneous SDO/AIA and Solar Orbiter/EUI-HRIEUV observations of slow waves in sunspot-anchored coronal fan feathers. In Event 1, the LoS are separated by 16.2 degrees, while in Event 2, they are almost parallel. Using time-distance analysis, we identify waves with periods in the 3-minute band and quantify wave decay using the exponential folding length. When LoS are non-parallel, the ratio of decay lengths measured by the two instruments, $λ_\mathrm{ratio} = λ_{\mathrm{AIA}} / λ_{\mathrm{EUI}}$ varies widely, with both $λ_\mathrm{ratio} > 1$ and $λ_\mathrm{ratio} < 1$ observed. However, when the LoS are almost parallel, the decay lengths agree with one another, and $λ_\mathrm{ratio} \approx 1$. These results show that the angle between the LoS and the wave propagation direction is key to determining the apparent decay of slow waves, a factor that has not yet been systematically accounted for. Since statistical studies of decay lengths constrain coronal energy-loss mechanisms, observational effects beyond simple projection must be corrected to reliably infer the underlying physical dissipation processes.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the apparent decay length of slow magnetoacoustic waves in the solar corona depends strongly on the angle between the line-of-sight (LoS) and wave propagation direction. When two instruments have parallel LoS, measured decay lengths agree; when non-parallel, they disagree. This projection effect must be corrected for reliable inference of coronal energy-loss mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing theories do not fully explain the wide range of observed decay lengths of slow magnetoacoustic waves in the solar corona, and measurements from different instruments frequently disagree. The authors aim to understand the cause of this discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors analyze two events with simultaneous SDO/AIA and Solar Orbiter/EUI-HRIEUV observations of slow waves in sunspot-anchored coronal fan feathers. Event 1 has LoS separated by 16.2°, Event 2 has nearly parallel LoS. Time-distance analysis identifies 3-minute period waves; decay is quantified via exponential folding length. Decay length ratios (λ_AIA/λ_EUI) are compared between the two configurations.
AI.result: When LoS are non-parallel (Event 1), the decay length ratio λ_ratio varies widely, with both >1 and <1 observed. When LoS are almost parallel (Event 2), decay lengths agree (λ_ratio ≈ 1). This demonstrates that the LoS angle relative to wave propagation direction is a key factor determining apparent wave decay.
AI.conclusion: The angle between line-of-sight and wave propagation direction critically affects apparent slow wave decay lengths. Observational effects beyond simple projection must be corrected to reliably infer physical dissipation processes from statistical decay-length studies.

title: V407 Vul: a triple star system with an AM CVn detectable by gravitational wave observatories
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Resubmitted to A&A after minor revision
summary: The AM CVn class includes mass transferring, ultra-compact double white dwarf binaries with orbital periods on the timescale of minutes. A long-standing puzzle is that none of the roughly fifty ultra-compact, "verification binaries" which are easily detectable in the millihertz gravitational wave regime reside in a triple star configuration. Much evidence has hinted at V407 Vul being an inspiraling, double white dwarf AM CVn with an orbital period of 569s. Yet, a decisive confirmation has proved challenging since a main sequence star dominates its visible spectrum. We present a clear confirmation of the triple star nature of the source by detecting a significant astrometric wobble of the photocentre on the 569s orbital period of the binary. The AM CVn and the main sequence components are gravitationally bound with a spatial separation of roughly 0.03-0.04'', equating to an orbital separation of approximately 120AU. A total of 23 years of orbital timing constrained the orbital decay of the AM CVn as being precise to the 1% level, critical in understanding if this class of binary survives through a period minimum or coalesce. New Hubble Space Telescope ultra-violet imaging and spectroscopic data allowed the isolated detection of the AM CVn at shorter wavelengths, revealing an approximately 58000 K accretor white dwarf, while placing a firm distance constraint of 3510+140-110 pc. At this distance, we predict that the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect V407 Vul with a 28.4+-9.2 signal-to-noise ratio in a 4yr mission time, making it the first verification binary with an outer tertiary, or "verification triple", detectable for millihertz gravitational wave observatories.

AI.tldr: V407 Vul is confirmed as the first triple-star system containing an ultra-compact AM CVn double white dwarf binary (569s orbital period) with a main sequence tertiary at ~120 AU separation. Long-term timing reveals precise orbital decay, HST data resolves the hot (~58,000 K) white dwarf accretor at 3510 pc, and LISA is predicted to detect it as the first "verification triple" for millihertz gravitational-wave observatories.
AI.motivation: None of the ~50 ultra-compact verification binaries detectable in the milliHz GW regime have been found in triple star systems, posing a long-standing puzzle. V407 Vul showed hints of being an AM CVn binary but lacked decisive confirmation due to a main sequence star dominating its optical spectrum.
AI.method: Astrometric wobble detection of the photocentre at the 569s orbital period; 23 years of orbital timing analysis; HST ultraviolet imaging and spectroscopy to isolate the AM CVn component at short wavelengths.
AI.result: Confirmed triple star nature; AM CVn and main sequence star separated by 0.03-0.04'' (~120 AU); orbital decay constrained to 1% precision; white dwarf accretor temperature ~58,000 K; distance 3510+140-110 pc; predicted LISA SNR 28.4 ± 9.2 in 4 years.
AI.conclusion: V407 Vul is the first "verification triple" – a triple-star system containing an ultra-compact binary detectable by millihertz GW observatories, resolving the puzzle of missing triples among verification binaries.

title: From simulations to observations of cool plasma: What we can learn from synthetic spectra
comment: 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Cool plasma of coronal rain or prominences and filaments is ubiquitous in the solar corona. We explored the synthetic spectra of MgII h&k lines in detail and analyse how well a non-adiabatic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of condensations in the corona matches observations when comparing the synthetic with the observed spectra. We applied, a Python implemented, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative-transfer framework, Promweaver to create synthetic spectra from a 2.5D MHD simulation created with MPI-AMRVAC. The simulation shows a dynamic system of numerous cold, dense thread-like structures that we compare to observations of the $\textit{Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph}$ (IRIS), with a focus on flare-driven coronal rain. We give a detailed description of the simulation from the aspect of the synthetic spectra. We show how and why the particular spectra form. A single thread already demonstrates great complexity. We further used the quartile analysis to systematically explore the evolution of observables in the observed and the synthetic spectra. This gives an overview of how the parameters change in time and that the changes seen in the simulation fit with the changes seen in observations. The results show that the simulation, in some aspects, matches particularly well to the observations of flare-driven coronal rain. Furthermore, we explored relations of parameters of the simulation and the observables. We find significant correlation between intensity and density, but not with temperature (in the studied temperature range of 5 to 20 kK). As a result, there is also a correlation of intensity and pressure. This relation allows us to further relate intensity and the vertical component of the Lorentz force. This brings us a step closer to a better understanding of the connection between the observed spectra and the atmosphere from which it originates.

AI.tldr: This paper compares synthetic MgII h&k spectra generated from a 2.5D non-adiabatic MHD simulation of coronal rain (using Promweaver non-LTE radiative transfer) with IRIS observations, finding good agreement for flare-driven coronal rain, and revealing correlations between intensity, density, pressure, and the Lorentz force.
AI.motivation: To understand how well non-adiabatic MHD simulations of coronal condensations reproduce observed spectra, and to bridge the gap between simulated atmospheric parameters and observed spectral signatures.
AI.method: Applied Promweaver (Python non-LTE radiative transfer) to a 2.5D MHD simulation from MPI-AMRVAC; performed quartile analysis to compare synthetic and observed IRIS spectra; explored parameter correlations.
AI.result: The simulation matches flare-driven coronal rain observations well; intensity correlates significantly with density and pressure but not with temperature in the 5–20 kK range; an intensity–Lorentz force relation is established.
AI.conclusion: The study advances understanding of how observed spectra relate to the underlying coronal rain atmosphere, enabling better interpretation of IRIS observations.

title: Project Hephaistos -- III. Characterizing anomalous infrared sources identified as Dyson-sphere candidates
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures
summary: The infrared-flux excess of stars harbouring Dyson spheres represent one potential technosignature of extraterrestrial intelligence. In a previous Project Hephaistos paper, we highlighted seven M dwarfs within 300 pc with unusual infrared properties that seem to resemble those expected for Dyson spheres. In the present study, we present an analysis of photometric and, in some cases, spectroscopic data on these seven objects, plus three additional objects with similar properties, to further constrain their nature. The stellar parameters, derived from calibrated empirical relationships for M dwarfs, reveal no irregularities with respect to the overall M-dwarf population of main-sequence stars. While the infrared properties of our targets resemble those of circumstellar disks in a transitional state, the objects with spectroscopic data show no signs of youth usually associated with such objects. One of our spectroscopic targets does exhibit weak H$α$ emission, but this is more likely attributed to stellar activity than to the gaseous accretion disk expected for a young star. After this analysis, we still find no clear explanation for the infrared excess of these stars, but note that observations with the JWST and/or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array would be able to probe scenarios in which the infrared excess is due to circumstellar dust emission or an infrared-bright background source that remains undetected at shorter wavelengths. For two of our stars, JWST observations have recently revealed superpositions with very red background galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 10 M dwarfs with infrared excess potentially indicative of Dyson spheres, finding no clear explanation for their unusual properties but suggesting further JWST/ALMA observations to distinguish between circumstellar dust, background sources, or other phenomena.
AI.motivation: To investigate M dwarfs with infrared excess that could represent Dyson sphere technosignatures, and to constrain the nature of these anomalous objects through photometric and spectroscopic analysis.
AI.method: Photometric and spectroscopic analysis of 10 M dwarfs (7 previously identified + 3 new) within 300 pc, using calibrated empirical relationships to derive stellar parameters and examine infrared properties.
AI.result: Stellar parameters are consistent with normal main-sequence M dwarfs; no youth indicators found in spectroscopic data; one weak Hα emission attributed to stellar activity; JWST observations for two stars revealed superpositions with red background galaxies.
AI.conclusion: No clear explanation for the infrared excess is found; further observations with JWST and ALMA are needed to differentiate between circumstellar dust, background sources, or other scenarios.

title: Herbig AeBe Star AS442A as a UXOR-type system
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables
summary: Detailed studies of the physical characteristics of young intermediate-mass Herbig Ae/Be (HAeBe) stars require extensive sets of homogeneous observational data collected over long periods. In this paper, we present the results of a multi-year study focusing on the faint Herbig Ae/Be star AS 442A. The goal of this study was to investigate the spectral and photometric variability of the star, utilizing long-term archival photometry alongside our own spectroscopic observations. The long-term photometric variability was statistically investigated using approximately 3,500 archival measurements spanning 1984 to 2025. Additionally, we examined the star's spectral variability using data obtained at the Shamakhy Astrophysical Observatory (ShAO) between 2020 and 2024. The three deepest brightness minima were detected in 1990, 2013, and 2023, with amplitudes of approximately ~2 mag in the U-band and up to ~1 mag in other bands. All three observed deep minima were accompanied by smaller brightness dips occurring both before and after the main event. The main light curve and color-magnitude diagrams show the "blueing" effect, which is characteristic of UXOR stars. A quasi-periodic occurrence of deep brightness minima with a period of P = 3759 +/- 35 days was detected for the first time. Our spectral observations were performed before the last deep light fading, which occurred in 2023. We show that the observed spectral variability, specifically the strengthening of emission lines and the reduction in depths and widths of absorption lines, is primarily related to the star's brightness variations. We have shown for the first time that the main reason for the UXOR-like brightness dip of the HAeBe star AS 442A can be explained by a periodic eclipse in a binary system. A close companion as a late-type secondary star with an orbit semimajor axis (a>7.5 au) likely drives the observed stellar variability.

AI.tldr: A multi-year study of the faint Herbig Ae/Be star AS 442A reveals UXOR-type photometric variability with ~2 mag U-band minima, a newly detected quasi-period of ~3759 days for deep minima, and evidence that the variability is caused by a periodic eclipse in a binary system with a late-type companion (semimajor axis >7.5 au).
AI.motivation: To investigate the spectral and photometric variability of the faint Herbig Ae/Be star AS 442A using long-term archival photometry (1984–2025, ~3,500 measurements) and new spectroscopic observations (2020–2024) to understand its physical characteristics and the mechanism driving its brightness dips.
AI.method: Long-term photometric variability was statistically analyzed using ~3,500 archival measurements from 1984–2025. Spectral variability was examined using spectroscopic data obtained at Shamakhy Astrophysical Observatory (ShAO) between 2020–2024. Light curve and color-magnitude diagram analyses were performed, including periodicity detection.
AI.result: Three deepest brightness minima detected in 1990, 2013, and 2023 (amplitudes ~2 mag U-band, ~1 mag other bands), each accompanied by smaller dips before/after. "Blueing" effect characteristic of UXOR stars observed. Quasi-periodic occurrence of deep minima with P = 3759 ± 35 days detected. Spectral variability (strengthened emission lines, reduced absorption line depths/widths) correlates with brightness variations.
AI.conclusion: The UXOR-like brightness dips of AS 442A are primarily explained by a periodic eclipse in a binary system with a close late-type companion (semimajor axis >7.5 au), which drives the observed stellar variability.

title: Toward 3D orbits of wide sdO/B binaries I. Six composite systems spatially resolved with VLTI/GRAVITY
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Hot subdwarf stars (sdO/Bs) are widely considered to be products of binary evolution. A significant fraction of them are found in long-period or wide binaries ($P>500$ d) with main sequence (MS) companions, likely resulting from a stable mass transfer episode where the MS companion stripped the hydrogen envelope of the sdO/B progenitor. Consequently, wide sdO/B binaries represent a key population in our pursuit of understanding stable mass transfer. They exhibit a modest range of orbital periods and eccentricities as revealed by long-term spectroscopic campaigns, though the component masses are not well constrained. In this Letter, we present the first long-baseline interferometry campaign to observe wide sdO/B + MS binaries and take the first step toward determining their 3-dimensional (3D) orbits and model-independent component masses. We target six composite sdO/B + MS systems with VLTI/GRAVITY and spatially resolve all of them. The projected physical separations range between $1-3$ au, with uncertainties between $1-8$%. When combined with complementary information from spectroscopic or astrometric observations, our precise measurements will be crucial to constrain 3D orbits for these systems. Additionally, we also identify a potential third component in BD+10 2357, although additional data will be necessary for confirmation. In light of continued spectroscopic monitoring and the imminent Gaia Data Release 4, we strongly encourage expanding the interferometric sample presented here to establish new, precise orbital and mass constraints for this key population of binary interaction products.

AI.tldr: This paper presents first long-baseline interferometry observations of six wide sdO/B + MS binaries using VLTI/GRAVITY, resolving all systems with projected separations of 1-3 au and uncertainties of 1-8%, enabling future 3D orbit and model-independent mass determinations. A potential third component is identified in BD+10 2357.
AI.motivation: Wide sdO/B binaries are key to understanding stable mass transfer in binary evolution, but their component masses are not well constrained due to limited orbital information.
AI.method: VLTI/GRAVITY long-baseline interferometry was used to observe six composite sdO/B + MS binaries, resolving all targets and measuring projected physical separations with high precision.
AI.result: All six systems were spatially resolved with projected separations of 1-3 au and uncertainties of 1-8%. A potential third component was identified in BD+10 2357.
AI.conclusion: These precise interferometric measurements, combined with spectroscopic and astrometric data, will enable 3D orbit determination and model-independent mass constraints. Expanding this sample is encouraged for future Gaia DR4 and ongoing spectroscopic monitoring.

title: JWST/MIRI Detection of Molecular H$_2$ Winds from an Edge-on Class II Source HV Tau C
comment: Accepted in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Journal. Main text: 25 pages with 13 figures
summary: The evolution of protoplanetary disks is regulated by accretion onto the central star and mass loss through jets and winds. While atomic and ionized outflows are commonly observed, molecular winds in evolved Class II disks remain rarely detected. We characterize the spatial, thermal, kinematic, and dynamical properties of molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) emission from the nearly edge-on Class II disk HV Tau C and assess the impact of its molecular wind. We also constrain accretion using H I recombination lines detected in the same mid-infrared spectrum. Using JWST/MIRI-MRS data from the MINDS Cycle 1 GTO program, we analyze spatially resolved pure-rotational H$_2$ emission. Rotational and position-velocity diagrams constrain excitation and kinematics, from which we estimate wind properties. We detect extended H$_2$ emission tracing a wide-angled, biconical molecular wind extending beyond the near-infrared scattered-light disk, ALMA 887 $μ$m dust continuum, and compact $^{12}$CO ($J=3$-$2$) gas disk. The H$_2$ rotational diagram requires warm ($\sim$600K) and hot ($\sim$2000K) components, similar to those in younger protostars. The gas shows outward motions of a few tens of km s$^{-1}$ and dynamical timescales of tens to hundreds of years. The inferred mass-loss rate is $\sim10^{-8}$ M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, while accretion rates derived from H I lines are $10^{-10}$-$10^{-8}$ M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. The accretion rate may be underestimated because of the edge-on geometry. Our results show that wide-angled molecular H$_2$ winds can persist into the Class II phase, with outflow rates comparable to some protostellar systems, suggesting that such winds may remain important for angular momentum removal, disk evolution, and dispersal. (Abstract modified; see the paper for the full version.)

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI-MRS observations of the edge-on Class II disk HV Tau C reveal extended warm (~600K) and hot (~2000K) molecular hydrogen (H2) emission tracing a wide-angled biconical wind, with mass-loss rate ~10⁻⁸ M☉/yr and accretion rates 10⁻¹⁰–10⁻⁸ M☉/yr, demonstrating that molecular winds persist into the Class II phase and may drive disk evolution.
AI.motivation: Molecular winds in evolved Class II disks are rarely detected, so their role in disk evolution and dispersal remains poorly understood. This study aims to characterize such a wind in HV Tau C to assess its impact.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI-MRS spatially resolved spectroscopy of pure-rotational H2 emission, combined with rotational and position-velocity diagrams to constrain excitation, kinematics, and wind properties. Accretion rates derived from H I recombination lines in the same mid-infrared spectrum.
AI.result: Extended H2 emission reveals a wide-angled biconical molecular wind extending beyond the scattered-light disk, ALMA dust continuum, and compact CO gas disk. Two temperature components (~600K and ~2000K) are found, with outflow speeds of tens of km/s, dynamical timescales of tens to hundreds of years, mass-loss rate ~10⁻⁸ M☉/yr, and accretion rates 10⁻¹⁰–10⁻⁸ M☉/yr (possibly underestimated due to edge-on geometry).
AI.conclusion: Wide-angled molecular H2 winds can persist into the Class II disk phase with outflow rates comparable to protostellar systems, suggesting they remain important for angular momentum removal, disk evolution, and dispersal.

title: High-Frequency Magnetohydrodynamic Waves with Substantial Energy in the Solar Polar Corona
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: The acceleration and heating of the fast solar wind remain long-standing challenges in space physics. One type of leading theoretical models requires high-frequency magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves to transport and dissipate sufficient energy in the corona. However, such high-frequency waves with energetically significant amplitudes have never been unambiguously observed, leaving a key gap between theories and observations. Using high-cadence, high-resolution extreme-ultraviolet imaging from Solar Orbiter's Extreme Ultraviolet Imager, we identify a previously hidden population of high-frequency MHD waves in coronal plumes of the solar polar region. An analysis of the detected propagating kink waves shows that over one-third have periods shorter than 100 s, a population largely undetected by earlier instruments. Power spectral analysis demonstrates that these high-frequency waves carry substantial energy flux, which are significantly underestimated in lower-cadence data. These results suggest that high-frequency MHD waves may contribute importantly to the energy budget of the solar polar corona and could play a role in solar wind acceleration, highlighting the value of high-resolution observations for probing energy transport in magnetized space and astrophysical plasmas.

AI.tldr: Using high-cadence EUV imaging from Solar Orbiter, the authors discover a previously hidden population of high-frequency MHD waves in coronal plumes, with over one-third having periods <100 s. These waves carry substantial energy flux, suggesting they may contribute importantly to coronal heating and solar wind acceleration, bridging a key gap between theory and observation.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing gap between theoretical models requiring high-frequency MHD waves for solar wind acceleration/heating and the lack of unambiguous observational evidence for such waves with energetically significant amplitudes.
AI.method: High-cadence, high-resolution extreme-ultraviolet imaging from Solar Orbiter's Extreme Ultraviolet Imager (EUI); detection and analysis of propagating kink waves in coronal plumes of the solar polar region; power spectral analysis of wave energy flux.
AI.result: Over one-third of detected kink waves have periods shorter than 100 s, a population largely missed by earlier instruments. These high-frequency waves carry substantial energy flux, significantly underestimated in lower-cadence data.
AI.conclusion: High-frequency MHD waves may contribute importantly to the energy budget of the solar polar corona and could play a role in solar wind acceleration, highlighting the value of high-resolution observations for probing energy transport in magnetized space and astrophysical plasmas.

title: Solar Wind Proton Heating and its Effect on Temperature Anisotropy Evolution between 0.05 and 1 au
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: This study focuses on the radial evolution of the solar wind proton adiabatic invariants and temperature anisotropies in the inner heliosphere. More specifically, we study in-situ measurements provided by the Parker Solar Probe, between 0.05 au and 0.25 au from the Sun, and Solar Orbiter spacecraft between 0.3 au and 1 au. Throughout the studied range of radial distances, we observe a significant average heating in the direction perpendicular to the local magnetic field for both fast and slow solar wind populations. On the other hand, there is no clear deviation from adiabaticity in the parallel direction regardless of the wind speed. The perpendicular heating is enough to significantly reduce the generation of the temperature anisotropy expected from a double adiabatic evolution. Despite the heating, an important portion of the solar wind (especially the slower wind streams) develops substantial anisotropies with higher parallel temperatures, which eventually become constrained by kinetic firehose instabilities.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter data (0.05-1 AU) to examine radial evolution of solar wind proton adiabatic invariants and temperature anisotropies. It finds significant perpendicular heating for both fast and slow solar wind, no clear parallel deviation from adiabaticity, and that perpendicular heating reduces expected double-adiabatic temperature anisotropy. Slower wind develops substantial parallel-dominated anisotropies constrained by firehose instabilities.
AI.motivation: To understand how solar wind proton adiabatic invariants and temperature anisotropies evolve radially in the inner heliosphere, and to characterize the heating processes and instability constraints affecting the solar wind plasma.
AI.method: In-situ measurements from Parker Solar Probe (0.05-0.25 au) and Solar Orbiter (0.3-1 au) were analyzed to study proton adiabatic invariants and temperature anisotropies as a function of radial distance, comparing fast and slow solar wind populations.
AI.result: Significant perpendicular heating was observed for both fast and slow solar wind, with no clear parallel deviation from adiabaticity. Perpendicular heating reduces the expected double-adiabatic temperature anisotropy. Slower wind streams develop substantial parallel-dominated anisotropies constrained by kinetic firehose instabilities.
AI.conclusion: Perpendicular heating plays a key role in modulating solar wind temperature anisotropy evolution, and firehose instabilities constrain anisotropy development particularly in slower wind streams.

title: Shear interaction and acceleration of a corotating stream detected by Parker Solar Probe
comment: 10 pages, Accepted in A&A
summary: Recent analysis of Parker Solar Probe (PSP) and Solar Orbiter data indicates that fluctuations energy is transferred to the bulk flow in fast streams of the solar wind at heliocentric distances between 15 and 120 Rsun. To gain insight into this process, we analyze data collected during the inbound orbit of PSP in Encounter 10, when it is in approximate corotation with the Sun and an accelerating stream is detected between 25 and 45 Rsun. The geometry of the flow indicates that a neighboring very fast streams is colliding with the corotating stream, causing large-scale magnetic field distortion, density enhancement, and acceleration. However, also deposition of fluctuations' energy can heat and do work on the solar wind plasma, resulting in a radial acceleration. We evaluate the energy lost by fluctuations via radial variation of conserved quantities in the corotating stream and find that it is almost equally partitioned into heating and work. While the heating is marginally consistent with the non-adiabatic decrease of proton temperature, the work exerted on the wind is insufficient to account for the measured solar wind acceleration. Although limited to this event, observations suggest that shear interaction is capable of accelerating slower streams within relatively short distances from the Sun, possibly leaving its imprint as large-scale density and magnetic fluctuations.

AI.tldr: Analysis of PSP data from Encounter 10 shows that while fluctuation energy is nearly equally partitioned into heating and work in a corotating solar wind stream between 25-45 Rsun, the work from fluctuations alone is insufficient to explain the observed acceleration, which appears driven primarily by shear interaction with a neighboring faster stream.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism behind solar wind acceleration in fast streams at heliocentric distances of 15-120 Rsun, where recent PSP/Solar Orbiter data show fluctuation energy being transferred to the bulk flow.
AI.method: Analysis of PSP inbound orbit data during Encounter 10 (25-45 Rsun), using radial variations of conserved quantities in a corotating stream to evaluate energy partitioning between heating and work, compared against measured proton temperature and acceleration.
AI.result: Fluctuation energy loss is nearly equally partitioned into heating and work; heating is marginally consistent with non-adiabatic proton temperature decrease, but the work term is insufficient to explain the observed acceleration. Shear interaction with a neighboring fast stream causes large-scale magnetic field distortion, density enhancement, and acceleration.
AI.conclusion: Shear interaction between streams is capable of accelerating slower streams at relatively short heliocentric distances, and the acceleration appears dominated by this process rather than fluctuation energy deposition, though shear interaction may leave imprints as large-scale density and magnetic fluctuations.

title: Progenitor models of supernovae interacting with their binary companions
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, submitted to the proceedings of IAU Symposium 406: Future landscape of astrophysical transients
summary: The appearance of nearly all core-collapse (CC) supernovae (SNe) is largely affected by the interaction between their progenitors and a close binary companion. Using a comprehensive, state-of-the-art grid of single- and binary stellar evolution models, the relative frequencies of SN types are predicted, as well as the distribution functions of their main properties. SNe that interact with nearby circumstellar material are included, namely those that explode during ongoing binary mass transfer, and are found to account for ~5% of all CCSNe, consistently with observations. The interaction between the newly born compact object and the companion is also investigated, which may produce observable signatures similar to those seen in SN2022jli. These SNe could account for between 3% and 27% of all H-poor CCSNe. These results will help develop strategies for identifying such supernovae in past and future searches, which will help to constrain uncertain physics in single and binary evolution models.

AI.tldr: Using binary stellar evolution models, this paper predicts that ~5% of core-collapse supernovae result from explosions during ongoing binary mass transfer, and 3-27% of H-poor CCSNe show signatures of compact object-companion interaction like SN2022jli.
AI.motivation: To understand how binary interactions affect the appearance and frequency of different core-collapse supernova types, and to quantify the role of close binary companions in shaping SN observational signatures.
AI.method: Comprehensive grid of single- and binary stellar evolution models, used to predict relative SN type frequencies and distribution functions of main properties.
AI.result: SNe exploding during ongoing binary mass transfer account for ~5% of all CCSNe; compact object-companion interaction SNe (similar to SN2022jli) account for 3-27% of H-poor CCSNe.
AI.conclusion: These results will guide observational strategies for identifying such SNe in past/future searches and help constrain uncertain physics in single and binary evolution models.

title: Exploring if a coronal dimming event can produce coronal hole-like properties
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Coronal dimmings, or transient coronal holes, are manifested as a sudden reduction in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and X-ray emission, often following solar eruptions. We investigate whether a dimming event can produce coronal hole-like plasma characteristics by comparing imaging and spectroscopic observations from Solar Orbiter, Hinode, IRIS, and SDO prior and during the dimming. The SDO/AIA 193 Å emission intensity in the dimming region was reduced to the same level as the neighbouring coronal hole within 11 hours. The Doppler velocity measured with Fe XII (corona) decreased from $-0.34^{+0.37}_{-0.27}$ km/s towards a predominant upflow of $-3.2^{+0.4}_{-0.6}$ km/s. The first ionisation potential (FIP) bias was reduced towards photospheric values. We found an increase in the number of automatically detected EUV brightenings near the dimming boundary in SDO/AIA 193 Å which could be a sign of magnetic reconnection. In the cooler SDO/AIA 171 Å or Solar Orbiter HRI_EUV 174 Å channel, we did not observe such an increase. Coronal bright points (CBPs) appeared relatively unaffected by the formation of the dimming. The Mg II $k_3$ (chromosphere) Doppler velocities were unchanged, except for a small reduction in the dimming upflows in areas with weak magnetic fields ($<20$ G). We find that the dimming only shows partial coronal hole-like properties; specifically, in the coronal emission lines and at temperatures of $>1$ MK. We suggest that this is due to the dimming resulting from plasma depletion only at higher altitudes. Since the CBPs were not significantly impacted by the dimming, we used their magnetic loop heights ($\sim 10$ Mm) as the lower limit to the dimming height. Our findings provide new insights into the atmospheric structure of coronal dimmings.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether coronal dimmings (transient coronal holes) develop full coronal hole-like plasma characteristics, finding that they only partially do so—showing coronal hole properties in high-temperature (>1 MK) emission and coronal Doppler shifts, but not in chromospheric lines or cooler channels—likely because the dimming results from plasma depletion at higher altitudes (>10 Mm), with coronal bright points used as a lower height limit.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a coronal dimming event can produce plasma characteristics similar to those of a coronal hole (reduced emission, upflows, low FIP bias), and to understand the vertical structure and formation mechanism of dimmings.
AI.method: Combined imaging and spectroscopic observations from Solar Orbiter (HRI_EUV 174 Å), Hinode (EIS), IRIS, and SDO (AIA 193/171 Å, HMI) before and during a dimming event; analysis of EUV intensity, Doppler velocities (Fe XII, Mg II k3), FIP bias, EUV brightenings, and coronal bright points.
AI.result: (1) Dimming intensity dropped to coronal hole levels within 11 hours in AIA 193 Å. (2) Coronal Doppler velocity shifted from near-zero to a predominant upflow of -3.2 km/s. (3) FIP bias decreased toward photospheric values. (4) EUV brightenings increased at dimming boundary in 193 Å but not in 171/174 Å. (5) Mg II chromospheric velocities unchanged except in weak-field areas. (6) Coronal bright points (CBPs) were unaffected, providing a ~10 Mm lower height limit for the dimming.
AI.conclusion: Coronal dimmings exhibit only partial coronal hole-like properties: the effect is confined to high-temperature coronal lines (>1 MK) and higher altitudes, while lower atmospheric layers (chromosphere, cooler EUV channels) remain largely unaffected. This suggests dimmings result from plasma depletion at altitudes >10 Mm rather than full opening of the magnetic field down to the chromosphere.

title: Binary-induced mass increase and helium enrichment of the envelopes of Type~IIP supernova progenitors
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, submitted to the proceedings of IAU Symposium 406: Future landscape of astrophysical transients
summary: Binary interactions are expected to play a major role in shaping the progenitor population of core-collapse supernovae, particularly in the era of deep, high-cadence transient surveys. Using ComBinE, a rapid binary population synthesis code combining tabulated stellar structure models with physically motivated mass-transfer stability criteria, we find that ~40% of Type II supernova progenitors at Milky Way metallicity originate from mergers between a post-main-sequence star and a main-sequence companion following unstable mass transfer. Compared to single-star progenitors with the same helium-core mass, these merger products have more massive hydrogen-rich envelopes and broader envelope-mass distributions. Their envelopes are helium-enriched, with relative enhancements of up to 80% and helium mass fractions reaching 0.4. These differences are expected to affect Type IIP light curves and should be considered in future progenitor and explosion models. Constraining the merger-induced Type IIP fraction with facilities such as LSST, Roman, and the ELT will provide insights into binary evolution physics.

AI.tldr: About 40% of Type II supernova progenitors at Milky Way metallicity come from stellar mergers following unstable mass transfer. These merger products have more massive, helium-enriched envelopes (up to 80% enhancement, He mass fractions reaching 0.4) compared to single-star progenitors, which will affect Type IIP light curves and should be considered in future models.
AI.motivation: Binary interactions are expected to significantly shape the progenitor population of core-collapse supernovae, especially with the advent of deep, high-cadence transient surveys. Understanding the role of mergers is crucial for interpreting observational data from upcoming facilities.
AI.method: Used ComBinE, a rapid binary population synthesis code that combines tabulated stellar structure models with physically motivated mass-transfer stability criteria, to simulate the progenitor population of core-collapse supernovae at Milky Way metallicity.
AI.result: Approximately 40% of Type II supernova progenitors originate from post-main-sequence star + main-sequence companion mergers. These merger products have more massive hydrogen-rich envelopes with broader mass distributions, and are helium-enriched (up to 80% enhancement, He mass fractions up to 0.4) compared to single-star progenitors with the same helium-core mass.
AI.conclusion: The differences in envelope mass and helium enrichment are expected to affect Type IIP light curves and should be incorporated into future progenitor and explosion models. Constraining the merger-induced Type IIP fraction using LSST, Roman, and the ELT will advance understanding of binary evolution physics.

title: A Citizen Science Search for Compact Emission Line Nebulae
comment: 14 pages, 22 figures, Appendix 1 table, accepted by Astronomische Nachrichten
summary: In recent years, citizen science became an integral part of astronomy. Numerous projects contribute to important studies by involving large communities. While these are getting quite some attention, there are also individual efforts, which are nevertheless very valuable. Here, we report on results of a search for compact optical emission line nebulae, which are signposts of both young and evolved stars. The increased brightness in red photometric bands due to the contribution of shock-excited emission lines has been used as a tracer when examining optical broadband surveys. With the help of public databases, we identified and characterized associated sources if possible. Most of them are young stellar objects (YSOs).

AI.tldr: A citizen science search using red photometric bands as tracers identified compact optical emission line nebulae, mostly young stellar objects (YSOs), from public databases.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the value of individual citizen science efforts in astronomy by searching for compact optical emission line nebulae, which are important signposts for both young and evolved stars.
AI.method: Used increased brightness in red photometric bands (due to shock-excited emission lines) as a tracer when examining optical broadband surveys, then identified and characterized associated sources using public databases.
AI.result: Identified and characterized compact optical emission line nebulae, with most being young stellar objects (YSOs).
AI.conclusion: Individual citizen science efforts complement large-scale projects and can effectively discover nebulae associated with young stars using broadband survey data.

title: A systematic assessment of the short-term X-ray behaviour of the $γ$ Cas analogues
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Context. Overall, $γ$ Cas analogues represent a class of OBe stars displaying bright and hard X-ray emission. This emission was recently determined to be the result of accretion onto a companion white dwarf (WD), which might possibly be a magnetic WD. Aims. We present a systematic review of the properties of $γ$ Cas analogues on short-term (kilosecond, ks) scales to further investigate the nature of the X-ray source. In particular, the presence of periodicities could be associated with the rotation of a magnetic WD. Methods. We generated the power spectra and a generalised Fourier algorithm. We applied an epoch folding method, along with Z2n approaches, to 131 X-ray detections of 26 $γ$ Cas analogues and two candidate sources. Results. We identified five sources ($γ$ Cas, $ζ$ Tau, HD45314, V771 Sgr, and $π$ Aqr), with recurrent periodic variability (P $\sim$ 1.2-5.4 ks) across observations. Period values and pulsed fractions are consistent with those reported for intermediate polars. However, while similar periods are found in all exposures of an object, the exact period value or folded light curve shape can vary. We also identify another nine sources displaying periodicities that cannot be confirmed, as there was only one observation available for their analysis. In other cases, periodicities appear (at best) transient and/or marginally significant. Aperiodic variability could be fitted by a power law in 18 of the sources, while the power-law index always is $\sim$ 1, as observed in other accreting WDs. Conclusions. The global properties of the observed short-term X-ray variability of the $γ$ Cas analogues are consistent with those observed from other accreting WD systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically analyzes short-term (kilosecond-scale) X-ray variability in γ Cas analogues (a class of OBe stars with bright, hard X-ray emission). Using Fourier, epoch folding, and Z²n methods on 131 X-ray detections of 26 sources, the authors find 5 sources (γ Cas, ζ Tau, HD45314, V771 Sgr, π Aqr) with recurrent periodic variability (P ~ 1.2–5.4 ks), consistent with intermediate polar white dwarfs. Nine additional sources show unconfirmed periodicities; others show transient or aperiodic power-law variability (index ~1). The global short-term X-ray variability properties align with accretion onto magnetic white dwarfs.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate the short-term (ks-scale) X-ray variability of γ Cas analogues to test the hypothesis that their X-ray emission arises from accretion onto a magnetic white dwarf companion, with periodic signals potentially tracing WD rotation.
AI.method: Generated power spectra and generalized Fourier algorithms; applied epoch folding and Z²n methods to 131 X-ray detections from 26 γ Cas analogues and 2 candidate sources.
AI.result: Five sources show recurrent periodic variability (P ~ 1.2–5.4 ks) consistent with intermediate polars; nine additional sources have unconfirmed single-observation periodicities; aperiodic variability follows a power law with index ~1 in 18 sources.
AI.conclusion: The short-term X-ray variability properties of γ Cas analogues are consistent with those of other accreting white dwarf systems, supporting the magnetic WD accretion scenario for the X-ray emission.

title: Understanding the Travel-time Asymmetry of Acoustic Waves in Sunspots With Time-distance Helioseismology
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: Mapping the subsurface structure and flow field of sunspots has been a challenging task for helioseismology. In this work, we investigate the propagation of acoustic waves in a sunspot in NOAA active region 11312 using time-distance helioseismology. Travel times of waves traveling into and out of the sunspot are measured as functions of travel distance and azimuthal angle relative to the local radial direction. The same time-distance analysis is also applied to a simulated data based on a magnetohydrostatic (MHS) model of sunspot, and forward modeling of travel times is performed using ray tracing based on both the MHS sunspot model and a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation. We find that both ingoing (traveling from the quiet area into the sunspot) and outgoing waves (traveling from the sunspot into the quiet area) have shorter travel times than in the quiet Sun, with travel-time reductions of up to 40 s. The magnitude of the mean time shift is largest for waves traveling along the radial direction at small travel distances. A clear asymmetry is detected between ingoing and outgoing waves: outgoing waves generally exhibit shorter travel times. This asymmetry is strongest for radial direction and small travel distances, with differences exceeding 1 min for 3.5 mHz and 4.5 mHz waves. From the results of both observations and models, our analysis indicates that the overall reduction in travel time could be primarily caused by the combined effects of Wilson depression, magnetic field, and wave-speed perturbations, while the ingoing-outgoing asymmetry could be partly attributable to subsurface flows. Although the forward-modeling results reproduce several qualitative features of the observations, quantitative discrepancies remain, highlighting limitations of current sunspot models and ray-theoretical approximations.

AI.tldr: This study investigates acoustic wave propagation in a sunspot (NOAA AR 11312) using time-distance helioseismology, finding travel-time reductions up to 40 s and ingoing-outgoing asymmetries exceeding 1 minute, with results suggesting causes include Wilson depression, magnetic fields, wave-speed perturbations, and subsurface flows, though quantitative discrepancies remain between observations and models.
AI.motivation: Mapping the subsurface structure and flow field of sunspots has been a challenging task for helioseismology, motivating this investigation into acoustic wave propagation to better understand sunspot interior dynamics.
AI.method: Time-distance helioseismology was applied to both observational data (NOAA AR 11312) and simulated data (MHS sunspot model). Travel times were measured as functions of travel distance and azimuthal angle. Forward modeling used ray tracing based on MHS and MHD models.
AI.result: Both ingoing and outgoing waves show travel-time reductions up to 40 s compared to quiet Sun. The mean time shift is largest for radial waves at small distances. A clear asymmetry exists: outgoing waves have shorter travel times than ingoing waves, exceeding 1 minute for 3.5 and 4.5 mHz waves radially at small distances.
AI.conclusion: Travel-time reductions are primarily caused by Wilson depression, magnetic fields, and wave-speed perturbations; ingoing-outgoing asymmetry may be partly due to subsurface flows. Current sunspot models and ray-theoretical approximations show limitations, as quantitative discrepancies persist between forward models and observations.

title: Automated Solar Radio Burst Detection Using Deep Learning on Augmented e-Callisto Data
summary: Solar radio bursts are signatures of energetic events associated with solar flares and coronal mass ejections and can interfere with terrestrial and space-based communication systems. Real-time automatic burst monitoring enables early warnings tens of minutes to hours before associated particles reach Earth and provides the basis for long-term statistical studies. The e-Callisto network is a worldwide system of solar radio spectrometers providing continuous observations, with its instruments collectively covering frequencies from approximately 20 MHz to 1 GHz. Burst detection and labeling currently rely largely on human experts, limiting scalability and real-time applicability due to hardware heterogeneity and low signal-to-noise ratios.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses solar radio burst monitoring using the e-Callisto network, highlighting the need for automated detection due to limitations of current human-dependent methods caused by hardware heterogeneity and low signal-to-noise ratios.
AI.motivation: To enable real-time automatic burst monitoring for early warnings (tens of minutes to hours before particle arrival) and scalable long-term statistical studies, replacing current human-expert-dependent labeling that limits real-time applicability.
AI.method: The e-Callisto network provides worldwide continuous solar radio observations from ~20 MHz to 1 GHz using heterogeneous hardware; the paper implies development of automated detection approaches to address challenges of hardware heterogeneity and low signal-to-noise ratios.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in abstract; the paper identifies limitations of current human-dependent detection but does not present specific results in this excerpt.
AI.conclusion: Automated burst monitoring is needed to overcome scalability and real-time constraints posed by human-dependent labeling in heterogeneous, low-SNR conditions across the e-Callisto network.

title: Long-Slit Spectroscopy Of Herbig-Haro Outflow System, Associated With IRAS 01166+6635
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Accepted by Reports of Nat.Acad.Sci. of Rep.Armenia
summary: We present long-slit spectroscopic observations of the outflow associated with an infrared source IRAS 01166+6635, conducted with the 6-m telescope of the Special Astrophysical Observatory using the SCORPIO-2 focal reducer. The structure of the flow as investigated in detail, its position-velocity diagrams are constructed. The electron densities of the several knots in the outflow were estimated, revealing a decrease in its density with increasing distance from the driving source.

AI.tldr: This paper presents long-slit spectroscopic observations of the outflow from IRAS 01166+6635 using the 6-m telescope with SCORPIO-2, analyzing its structure via position-velocity diagrams and finding that electron density decreases with distance from the driving source.
AI.motivation: To investigate the detailed structure and physical properties (particularly density distribution) of the outflow associated with the infrared source IRAS 01166+6635.
AI.method: Long-slit spectroscopic observations using the 6-m telescope of the Special Astrophysical Observatory equipped with the SCORPIO-2 focal reducer; construction of position-velocity diagrams; estimation of electron densities in outflow knots.
AI.result: Electron densities of several knots in the outflow were estimated, showing a systematic decrease in density with increasing distance from the driving source.
AI.conclusion: The outflow from IRAS 01166+6635 exhibits a density gradient where electron density decreases as distance from the central driving source increases, consistent with an expanding or dissipating outflow structure.
